native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Among the two groups in this dataset, the Lower-middle-income (LMC) aggregate shows the larger and better-supported positive association between rising education expenditure and per-capita output, and Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) shows the weaker one - though the association is far weaker than raw levels fits suggest and is not robust enough for a causal claim. Using the only available proxies (outcome = GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$, rather than the brief's 'GDP, 2010 US$'; exposure = 'Adjusted savings: education expenditure', % of GNI, not a government budget share; 'developing countries' = the LMC aggregate), a one-percentage-point rise in the share of GNI directed to education is associated with about +1.5 percentage points of annual per-capita growth in LMC countries (b=+0.0151, SE=0.0056, t=2.70, n=40, Newey-West(4)), whereas for SSA the slope is unstable and not distinguishable from zero (b=-0.0516, SE=0.0236, n=4 without controls; sign flips to +0.0408, SE=0.0330, t=1.24 once export growth is added; n=4 because SSA per-capita output exists only for 2011-2015). That SSA ordering is bounded: the LMC positive slope reverses under a two-year distributed lag (cumulative -0.0193, t=-0.73), vanishes in 1991-2015 (-0.0312, t=-0.70), and hinges on one year (dropping 1976 gives +0.0017; block-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.010,+0.033], p=0.16). The Delta-education x SSA interaction is not interpretable (4 of 44 rows are SSA; Chow F(2,40)=0.134, p=0.875), so equal slopes can be neither established nor rejected. Descriptively SSA sustained a HIGHER education-investment share than LMC (+0.80 pp of GNI on average 1975-2015; +0.25 pp in 2011-2015) while ending 2015 LOWER in per-capita output ($1,634 vs $1,965), slower-growing (1.24%/yr vs 2.01%/yr) and far behind in secondary enrollment (gross 43.4 vs 64.5), so higher education spending in SSA is associated with no relative per-capita-output advantage. Levels regressions appearing to show large negative effects (LMC edu -0.2002, t=-3.04, R2=0.92) are spurious common-trend artifacts (DW=0.52). All estimates are associations from two overlapping WDI aggregate series in which the exposure's denominator is the outcome, leaving reverse causality and mechanical-share effects unresolved.
native_result.WorkflowB: Wide WDI reshape -> tidy 2x41 panel (analysis/panel_tidy.csv) -> coverage/missingness audit -> primary first-differenced growth models with Newey-West(4) SEs per group -> distributed-lag and cumulative-effect test -> levels contrast flagged as spurious (DW=0.52) -> interaction + Chow test with classical-vs-HAC SE comparison -> 13-variant robustness table -> leave-one-year-out and stationary block bootstrap (20k reps) -> enrollment/level descriptives as mechanism evidence. Staged file only; no external data; associational framing throughout.
